| D78 | The spectator view is `redactGame(..., spectating)` — one gate, both sides symmetric (P4 online, increment 3c-vii-a) | Spectate is the last item on the P4 plan, and it splits cleanly: this is the HIDDEN-INFORMATION half, landed on its own so it can be reviewed as a security change rather than buried in transport and UI (the 2b-iii-a precedent — the seam before its consumer). **The threat model is the decision.** A spectator is not a stranger: the realistic attacker is a PLAYER who opens a spectator view of the match they are playing to read the other hand. So the property is "a spectator sees strictly LESS than either seated player", and the two sides are treated symmetrically — `redactGame(state, side, true)` withholds BOTH hands, BOTH sides' setup placements (a seated viewer sees their own because they placed them; a spectator placed nothing, so watching from p1's side must not reveal what p1 benched) and every actor affordance. `viewerSeat` degrades from "who I am" to "which side renders at the bottom". **The mechanism matters as much as the rule:** the five `turn:action` affordance helpers already guarded on `viewerSeat !== turnSeat`, so widening that parameter to `Seat | null` and passing ONE `actor = spectating ? null : phase.seat` withholds all five through guards that already existed — rather than five `spectating ? [] : …` branches that the next affordance added there could silently miss. That is not tidiness: `trainers`/`abilities`/`rareCandy` name cards **in the actor's hand**, so leaking them would undo the hand redaction two lines above. The `effect:choose` prompt is withheld the same way (its candidates can be the answerer's own deck cards, and a spectator can never answer). What still crosses is exactly what is public at a real table: both boards after setup, the Stadium, discards, prize/deck COUNTS, hand SIZES, whose turn it is and the outcome. Alternatives rejected: a separate `redactForSpectator` that post-processes a seated snapshot (fragile — a new leaky field passes straight through unless someone remembers to strip it), and letting a spectator see both hands behind a "trusted spectator" flag (there is no such thing when either player can open the link). engine RULES UNCHANGED (0.41.0 — a read surface, not a rules surface; `MATCH_RECORD_VERSION` untouched since neither `GameState` nor the record moved). 1858 → **1865** tests, including the one that matters: no uid private to EITHER seat appears anywhere in a spectator snapshot, asserted from both sides of the table. **NOT WIRED YET** — nothing calls it until 3c-vii-b, which is deliberately scoped to reuse the lobby link as the spectate link: a third socket whose `hello` is `reject-full` becomes a spectator IF the lobby is in-game (you can watch a match, you cannot watch a lobby), which needs no new frame and no new URL. *Why: the safe default has to be structural. Anyone can add a field to `RedactedPhase` next month; the only way that field is withheld from a spectator by default is if the withholding lives at the one place the actor is decided, not at each field.* (2026-07-26) |

| D79 | The lobby link IS the spectate link — a refused seat becomes a spectator (P4 online, increment 3c-vii-b) | Wiring 3c-vii-a's seatless redaction to real viewers, with the design constraint that it add **no new frame, no new URL and no invite flow**. The entry point is a refusal that already existed: `helloDecision` returns `reject-full` to a third player, and that branch now — **only while the lobby is `in-game`** — also marks the socket a spectator (`attachSpectator`, attachment.ts) and hands it the snapshot plus `redactGame(state, "p1", true)`. The rule falls out of the code rather than being imposed on it: **you can watch a MATCH, you cannot watch a lobby.** Outside in-game the refusal stays the dead end it has always been, which is right — a pre-match lobby has nothing to show, and a seat may yet free up for that person. **A spectator is deliberately not a participant in any sense the lobby can see:** no `playerId`, no `PlayerState`, nothing in the snapshot, so no rule anywhere depends on how many are watching, and the reducer is untouched. Their safety is structural twice over — every handler that can change the game gates on `attachedPlayer`, which stays null for them, and the board they receive is the one that withholds both hands. `attachPlayer` clears the flag, so a watcher who later takes a freed seat stops getting the seatless board. **Players are NOT told they are being watched** — chosen deliberately: telling them needs a spectator count on the wire and a broadcast on every join/leave, and the lobby already treats a refused socket silently. Recorded here so the next session can reverse it knowingly rather than discover it. **Deliberate consequence:** anyone with (or guessing) a 4-character lobby code can watch a game in progress. What they get is a public table — both boards, no hands, no deck order, no prizes — which is the intended product behaviour, not an oversight. **Client:** `useLobby`'s sticky `rejected` boolean became `refusal: "full" | "kicked" | null`, because the two are no longer the same thing — a KICK is terminal, while "full" keeps the connection, keeps accepting `state` (for the players' names) and `match` (the board), and flips the status to `spectating` on the first board. Its hello retry moved to the idle-driven cadence heartbeats already keep fresh, so a spectator whose socket drops re-announces and is re-marked, without becoming a retry storm against a lobby that is simply full. `OnlineMatch` gained `spectating`, which removes every control (`OnlineHud`, Concede, Rematch, drags, Pass, the forfeit banner), keeps the board, the LOG and the result, and asks a leave question that costs nothing. 1865 → **1874** tests. **BROWSER-VERIFIED with a third, signed-out profile on the same lobby link:** the board rendered; at `setup:place` the player saw their own hand as "Skeledirge; Skeledirge; Rare Candy; …" while the spectator saw "Face-down card" ×7 for BOTH hands — the hidden-information property, live; the spectator had no Concede/Ready/Rematch and a disabled Pass; a concede propagated to them instantly with the result but no Rematch; a rematch dropped them back to "Lobby is full" (the watch-a-match-not-a-lobby rule); and they picked the NEXT match up automatically when it started. Zero page errors on all three. **The run caught a real bug:** `state` frames only go out on a lobby COMMIT, so a spectator joining mid-match never received one and their board read "Host vs Guest" — `refuseSeat` now sends the snapshot explicitly. *Why: the cheapest correct entry point is one that already exists. "Refused a seat" and "may watch" are the same fact about a socket, so deriving one from the other costs a branch instead of a protocol, and the rule it implies — matches are watchable, lobbies are not — is the one you would have chosen anyway.* (2026-07-26) |

| D80 | Half-open sockets are swept with the runtime's OWN keepalive timestamp (P4 online, increment 3c-viii) | The gap 3c-v's browser run surfaced, and the last known way an online match could stall. `setWebSocketAutoResponse` answers the client's 1.5s ping without waking the DO — the thing that makes hibernation worth having — but it also means the DO can never notice pings that STOP. A network that dies without a TCP close therefore left a socket that looked perfectly live forever: `hasSocket` said yes, no disconnect grace was armed, no forfeit clock started, and the opponent waited indefinitely. Every ORDINARY exit (tab close, browser kill, navigation, reload, crash) delivers a close event, which is why this never bit in practice and why it took a deliberate `set offline` to reproduce. **The fix is to read the signal the runtime was already recording:** `state.getWebSocketAutoResponseTimestamp(ws)` returns when it last auto-answered that socket, so liveness costs nothing at ping time. The alternative — dropping the auto-response and stamping `lastSeen` in `webSocketMessage` — was rejected on exactly that ground: it would wake the DO ~40 times a minute per socket and give up hibernation to learn what the runtime already knows. **What it costs instead is a POLL**, because a quiet in-game lobby schedules no alarm at all: `scheduleMaintenance` now pushes a `LIVENESS_SWEEP_MS` (30s) deadline whenever any socket is connected, so an occupied lobby wakes twice a minute. `SOCKET_SILENCE_MS` is 15s — ten missed pings, so a phone changing networks or a throttled background tab is not mistaken for a dead one — and a test pins the budget that matters: sweep + silence + the 5s grace all fit inside the 90s forfeit, so a dead network can never resolve slower than a closed tab. **A `null` timestamp counts as ALIVE**, deliberately: it is the state of every connection before its first ping, and nothing can distinguish "just opened" from "opened long ago and never pinged" — the cost of that reading is a socket we never sweep, versus closing a healthy one-second-old connection. **The sweep only CLOSES**; everything after it — the grace, the seat going disconnected, the forfeit — is the machinery a real close already drives, reached through the same `socketGone` (called explicitly, since a server-side `close()` delivers no `webSocketClose` event to us). 1874 → **1878** tests. **BROWSER-VERIFIED with the very reproducer that exposed the bug:** with a match live, one client was put offline with the socket left open; before this change that produced nothing at all, and now the opponent saw "disconnected — forfeits in 1:30" after ~50s (15s silence + up to 30s sweep + the 5s grace) and the countdown ran. Bringing the client back online restored it within ~10s — the channel reconnected, re-helloed, and the forfeit was cancelled — while the client that stayed connected throughout was never swept. Zero page errors. *Why: the cheapest signal is the one someone else is already recording. Hibernation exists to avoid waking on keepalives, so any fix that inspects keepalives directly is self-defeating; asking the runtime when it last answered turns a per-ping cost into a per-half-minute one.* (2026-07-26) |

| D81 | A lobby seat's name is the ACCOUNT's, resolved server-side (P5 polish, increment P5-1) | The first P5 item, and the one a player notices before anything else: after twelve P4 increments the lobby still said "Player 6046". A seat's name was whatever the client announced in its `hello` — a handle generated into localStorage, editable by anyone, belonging to nobody. It is now the account's `displayName`, read at the hello by `loadDisplayName` from the same `userId` the /ws session cookie already resolved (the second use of the lobby's one authenticated fact, after the owner-scoped deck read). **Resolving rather than trusting is the decision**, and it is not only cosmetic: the moment names stop being random, a client-supplied name is an impersonation vector — announce yourself as your opponent's handle and the versus screen agrees. The read sits deliberately AFTER the refusal branches, so a socket that gets no seat costs no D1 query however often it retries, and hellos are rare in steady state (heartbeats keep the client's idle timer fresh, so it only re-announces after a real gap). **The fallback rule is the careful part:** a blank account name yields `null`, and the caller drops back to the client's announced handle — never to the EMAIL, which is the one substitution that suggests itself because `AccountButton` uses exactly that. That control shows a user their OWN address; a lobby name is broadcast to the opponent and, since 3c-vii, to spectators. A cosmetic blank is a smaller problem than a published email address, and a test pins it. The client announces its account name as well, which changes nothing authoritative — it only spares the host the half-second where their own seat reads "Player 4271" before the first broadcast corrects it, since the waiting screen is seeded locally. No server-side length cap: registration bounds names at 64, `PlayerPanel` already truncates, and mangling someone's name to fit a panel is the UI's job, not the wire's. 1878 → **1881** tests, `bun run check` green. **BROWSER-VERIFIED on four clients:** two signed-in seats read "Ash" and "Misty" across the player panels, the turn banner, the game log ("Ash wins the toss") and the spectator pill ("Watching — Ash vs Misty"), while two SIGNED-OUT players kept their generated handles with the lobby working normally. Zero page errors. *Why: a name is identity, and identity that the client asserts is not identity at all. The server already knew who the socket was — using that costs one query and closes an impersonation hole that only existed because nobody's name meant anything yet.* (2026-07-26) |

| D82 | Generated avatars from a hashed account id, not uploads (P5 polish, increment P5-2) | The other half of "lobby identity", and split from the uploads polish.md describes on purpose: an upload flow means R2, a CSP change, moderation questions and a settings surface, while what the lobby actually lacked was any face at all — `PlayerPanel` drew the same grey figure for everyone. **A generated avatar buys most of the value for none of that infrastructure:** `PlayerState.avatarSeed` carries a token the server derives at the hello from the account behind the socket, and `PlayerAvatar` draws a deterministic two-hue gradient with the account's initial. Nothing is stored, nothing is uploaded, and the property that matters holds — the same person looks the same to you in every lobby, which is what makes it identity rather than decoration (browser-verified across two clients: both saw identical gradients for the same accounts, in opposite seats). **It is a HASH of the account id, never the id.** Not because a uuid is guessable, but because the lobby snapshot is BROADCAST — to the opponent, and since 3c-vii to spectators — and an internal primary key is the wrong thing to publish there: it invites joining this seat to any other surface exposing the same id. FNV-1a is enough because this is a display token, not a security boundary; the client's only use is picking colours. **An anonymous seat gets NO seed and keeps the generic figure**, deliberately: the only id available for one is the per-lobby playerId, and a face derived from that would change on the player's next visit — promising an identity that isn't there is worse than admitting there is none. **Saturation and lightness are fixed**, so the seed picks the hue and never how loud the result is; that is what stops one player's face glowing next to another's in a UI built on restrained glass. An empty name draws a bare gradient rather than a placeholder letter, since a wrong initial is a claim and a gradient is not. The wire field cost one line in `readSnapshot`'s `withSeatDefaults` — the normalizer 3c-v added for exactly this, so a lobby persisted by the previous deploy survives the new field instead of being evicted. 1881 → **1889** tests. **BROWSER-VERIFIED on four clients:** two signed-in seats drew stable, visually distinct faces ("A" orange→amber, "M" cyan→indigo) with byte-identical gradients on both clients, and two signed-out seats kept the generic figure. A screenshot confirmed they sit in-palette against both the blue and red seat washes. *Why: the expensive half of avatars is storage and moderation; the valuable half is that people become recognisable. Deriving a face from the account you already authenticated delivers the second without buying the first, and leaves the upload path a strict improvement rather than a rewrite.* (2026-07-26) |

| D83 | A deck's cover is its highest-HP Pokémon, derived on read (P5 polish, increment P5-3) | The decks grid drew the same blue card back for every deck under a generated tint, while the catalog has had real scans since P2. **The slice's whole content is the RULE**, so it lives in a pure `pickCoverCardId` that can be argued with and tested rather than inside SQL: **the Pokémon with the highest printed HP**, ties broken by copies, then by card id for determinism. HP is the best proxy the catalog offers for "the card this deck is built around", and crucially it is one number rather than a taxonomy to interpret — an ex/V/VMAX or a Stage 2 outranks the Basics that fetch it WITHOUT anyone having to rank `stage` values against each other. The two obvious alternatives both fail on a real deck: ranking by STAGE gets a Basic-ex deck wrong (a 330 HP Basic ex is the payoff and would lose to any Stage 2 tech line), and ranking by COUNT gets nearly every evolution deck wrong (the 4-of Basic beats the 3-of Stage 2 it evolves into — verified live: Skeledirge ×3 correctly beat Fuecoco ×4). Cards with no scan are skipped rather than picked and rendered blank, and a deck with no qualifying card gets `coverCardId: null`, keeping the card back — which is also exactly right for a deck you have only just created (`fromDeck`, the create-response mapper, hardcodes null for that reason). **Derived on READ**, in one extra query for the whole library beside the existing `cardCount` aggregate: no stored column, so a cover follows the deck's contents with nothing to keep in sync, and no write path to change. It is a HEURISTIC and will occasionally pick a wall over the attacker beside it; the proper answer is letting the owner choose, which this leaves room for (a stored choice would simply win over it). **A browser run caught what tests could not:** the deck NAME, white text that had always sat on a flat blue back, was nearly illegible over flames and holo foil — so the label gained a gradient scrim, applied ONLY when there is art, so a coverless deck looks exactly as it did. 1889 → **1899** tests. *Why: the cheapest correct default beats a configuration surface nobody has asked for yet, and HP is the rare heuristic that is both trivially cheap and right on the decks that matter.* (2026-07-26) |

Second, the ⟶ pass control is enabled **exactly when the turn panel renders over it** — the panel appears precisely when `passDisabled === false` — so on /play and online it was never clickable, and relocating it would have been moving a control whose replacement (each panel's own `Pass`) already exists and is browser-verified. **The API expresses the rule instead of a flag:** `PlaymatView.onPassTurn` became OPTIONAL, and the control renders only for a driver that passes one — "give the board a pass control by giving it something to call". The /simulator sandbox passes one (nothing covers it there); /play and online do not, and shed their now-dead `passTurn`/`passDisabled` wiring with it. | D85 | Your account is editable on /settings, and the avatar seed rides on `User` (P5 polish, increment P5-5) | P5-1 made a lobby seat's name the ACCOUNT's `displayName`, resolved server-side and broadcast to the opponent and to spectators — and left a player wearing whatever register picked, with nowhere to change it. **`PATCH /auth/me` + a Profile section on /settings** closes that: one required field (`updateProfileRequestSchema`, trim + 1–64, the same bounds register uses on its OPTIONAL name), `requireUser` BEFORE the validator so a signed-out caller hears "unauthorized" rather than a critique of their body, and no write at all when the name is unchanged. **The interesting decision is the FACE.** A profile that showed a name but no avatar would be a text box calling itself a profile, and one drawing a lookalike avatar would be worse — it would promise a face that isn't the one opponents see. So `userSchema` gained **`avatarSeed`**, derived by the same `avatarSeedFrom` D82 introduced, and the section renders the SAME `PlayerAvatar` the lobby does. That moved two things deliberately: the module to `apps/api/src/auth/avatar.ts` (the seed is a property of the ACCOUNT, not of a seat — lobby already imports from auth, not the reverse) and the component to `src/components/` (shared, so /settings and the lobby cannot drift into two similar drawings). A test pins `avatarSeedOf` against `avatarSeedFrom` for the same reason. **Deriving the seed client-side was rejected**: a second copy of FNV-1a in the web bundle is a hash that must agree with the server forever, and the day it doesn't a player's own face silently stops matching the one everyone else sees. Publishing it costs nothing — the lobby already broadcasts it. Smaller calls: the avatar's initial follows the DRAFT as you type, so the face and the field can never disagree on screen; a 401 on save re-probes the session so the panel becomes the sign-in prompt, which says it better than an error line under a dead form; the form is keyed by `user.id` so switching accounts re-seeds the field. A rename reaches a lobby at the next hello (`loadDisplayName` resolves the seat name there), so a player already seated elsewhere keeps the old name until they rejoin. 1899 → **1911** tests. **BROWSER-VERIFIED on two clients:** renaming "Brock" → "Pewter Brock" flipped the initial to "P" live, kept the gradient byte-identical (the seed is the account id, not the name), updated the corner account control with no reload, survived a reload, and — the point of the slice — **the opponent's client showed "Pewter Brock" with that same gradient**. | D86 | A deck cover is a PIN over the derived default, resolved on read (P5 polish, increment P5-6) | P5-3 fronted every deck with its highest-HP Pokémon and said outright that the proper answer was letting the owner choose. This is that: a nullable `decks.cover_card_id` the editor sets, and a pure **`effectiveCoverCardId(chosen, candidates)`** the list query runs — **the pin wins, and everything else falls through to `pickCoverCardId`**. The derived rule is untouched; it is now explicitly the DEFAULT rather than the answer. **Three decisions carry the slice.** First, **the resolution runs against the candidate list the default was already deriving from**, so honouring a choice costs NO extra query, and a pin that has gone stale (its card removed elsewhere, or its scan gone after a re-ingest) silently falls back instead of drawing a blank rectangle — a deck must never front a card it doesn't run. Second, **the pin may be a TRAINER or an Energy while the derived default stays Pokémon-only**: guessing needs a rule, choosing does not, and a signature Supporter is a legitimate face (browser-verified with Academy at Night, which the rule could never pick). Third, **two fields, deliberately not one**: `DeckSummary.coverCardId` remains the face being DRAWN (so the grid needed no change at all), while the full `Deck` carries `chosenCoverCardId`, the stored CHOICE the editor's picker is set to — null for almost every deck. Collapsing them into one name would have made "what is drawn" and "what was chosen" the same word for two different questions. **`Automatic` is an explicit option in the picker**, not the absence of one, so reverting is one click; it deliberately shows no art, because the default is a RULE and drawing today's answer to it would read as "this card". **The consistency rule lives on both sides:** PATCH validates the pin against the card list the patch LEAVES BEHIND (400 `cover card not in deck`) and drops a pin whose card that patch removes, while the editor's `toSnapshot` drops it locally too — not cosmetic, since the cover rides the same debounced PATCH as the card list, and a self-contradicting body would 400 forever (the saver retries the same dirty snapshot). The cover joining that one save path is what keeps the pair atomic. 1911 → **1932** tests; migration `0004`. **BROWSER-VERIFIED end to end at 1920×1080:** pinning the Trainer put it on the library tile, removing it dropped the pin, kept saving ("Saved", PATCH 200 — the wedge that would have followed a naive implementation) and fell back to Absol; a pin survived a reload through GET /decks/:id; a hand-crafted PATCH naming a card outside the deck got the 400; and both the footer control and a picker tile hit-tested to themselves. *Why: a heuristic that is right most of the time plus an override that is always right beats trying to make the heuristic cleverer — and the override is only trustworthy if the two can never disagree about what the deck contains.* (2026-07-26) |
| D87 | A favourite deck is a validated PIN of the account's OWN deck, resolved on read (P5 polish, increment P5-7) | Joins P5-5 (an editable profile) and P5-6 (a deck's cover art): an account pins one of its own decks as its favourite and sees that deck's cover + name on /settings. A nullable **`users.favourite_deck_id`** (migration `0005`) surfaced as **`userSchema.favouriteDeckId`** — **just the ID.** **Three choices.** First, **store only the id, not the deck's name/cover:** /settings resolves those from the caller's own `GET /decks` list, so a rename or re-cover shows through with no stale copy and a favourite whose deck has vanished resolves to a blank tile — the SAME "derive on read, tolerate stale" the covers use (D83/D86). Second, **a favourite must be one of YOUR decks:** `PATCH /auth/me` gains an OPTIONAL nullable `favouriteDeckId` (absent leaves it, null clears it, a string is validated against the caller's decks) and 400s `favourite deck not found` for anyone else's id or a phantom — the account can never point at a deck it doesn't own, mirroring D86's `cover card not in deck`. Third, **the FK is `ON DELETE SET NULL`** so deleting a favourited deck clears the pin rather than blocking the delete (a RESTRICT FK would) or dangling a stale id; D1 enforces FKs here (the deck DELETE leans on `deck_cards`' cascade), and since drizzle-kit drops the referential action on an ADD COLUMN, migration 0005 restores `ON DELETE SET NULL` by hand. The users↔decks mutual reference forced an `AnySQLiteColumn` annotation to break the TS type cycle. The picker is a native `<select>` in the SAME form as the name, riding ONE PATCH so name + favourite save atomically; the provider adopts the answer, so the corner control follows with no re-probe. 1932 → **1936** tests. Browser-verified end to end 2026-07-27 (build #71): pin on /settings → cover (`sv06.5-012`, real art) + name render + `PATCH /auth/me` 200; survives reload; `DELETE`ing the deck clears `favouriteDeckId` to null server-side (the FK) and the tile goes blank. | D88 | A card detail view is a read-only modal hydrated on demand from the full-card endpoint (P5 polish, increment P5-8) | Cards in the deck builder had only ever been an add-a-copy tile; this adds a **detail modal** opened from the grid that shows the full card (attacks, abilities, weakness/resistance/retreat, illustrator, rarity, regulation mark, Trainer/Energy rules text). The backend was already complete — a `GET /cards/:id` returning the full `cardSchema`, and a battle-tested `getCard` client — so the whole slice is web-UI; nothing in API/DB/schema/ingest changed. **Four decisions.** First, **the inspect affordance is a SIBLING of the add button, never a child:** the grid tile is a `<button>` (click adds, right-click removes, pointer-down drags) and a button-in-button is invalid HTML, so a corner info button floats over the tile at `z-20`, revealed on tile hover and its own keyboard focus; clicking it opens the modal and does NOT add a copy, and the three existing tile gestures are untouched. Second, **seed + fetch, and the fetch must never blank the seed:** the header name and big image come from the `BuilderCard` the grid already holds (up the instant the dialog opens) while the body swaps loading→ready as `getCard` resolves; a `cancelled` flag drops a stale response so reopening a different card can't be clobbered by a slower earlier fetch, and the seed is retained through the close so nothing flashes empty. Third, **honest about what the catalog stores:** pricing, national-dex number and flavor text are NOT in D1 (see the `cards` schema header), so the view doesn't show them, and the set prints as raw `{localId} · {setId}` rather than a name lookup the payload can't back; every block is guarded so a Trainer/Energy omits what it lacks. Fourth, **the new surface respects `prefers-reduced-motion`** (`motion-reduce:transition-none`, no scale under reduced motion) — a down-payment on the reduced-motion-audit item, and the model the older P5 surfaces (CoverDialog, PlayerAvatar) still need. Type/cost pips reuse `EnergyGlyph` behind a pure exported `isGlyphType` guard that text-chips anything outside the ten glyph keys. 1936 → **1941** tests (a jsdom dialog test + the guard). Built via sub-agents; main session reviewed the diff — self-reviewed, no independent reviewer. **BROWSER-VERIFIED end to end 2026-07-27 (build #72):** hover revealed the corner button; clicking "View Absol details" opened the modal (name instant) then `GET /cards/:id` (200) filled Attacks/Combat/Illus + a high-quality `<img>` (`naturalWidth=600`) from the R2 mirror; the info click left "Add Absol" at 0-in-deck; a Trainer refetched to show only its Effect; X/Escape/backdrop all closed it; zero console errors. *Why: the data already existed one endpoint away — the only real question was interaction, and making inspect a peer of add (not a mode on it) keeps the fast add-a-copy loop intact while giving the card a place to be read; hydrate-on-open with a stale-guard is the same "derive on read" discipline the rest of P5 uses, and refusing to invent pricing/set-name keeps the view trustworthy.* (2026-07-27) |

Halting the spin is the correct accessible behaviour: the "Save" text plus the disabled/dimmed button already convey the in-progress state, and `SpinnerIcon` is a 3/4-ring arc that reads fine frozen. Pure CSS-class slice — no logic, component, or API/DB/schema touch; 1941 → 1941 tests (nothing new to unit-test: `motion-reduce:*` variants aren't observable in jsdom and asserting className strings is brittle). `bun run check` green (137 files / 1941 tests); engine rules unchanged (0.41.0). **Verified via the shipped stylesheet, not a browser drive:** a production `vite build` emits BOTH `motion-reduce:transition-none` and `motion-reduce:animate-none` inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`, proving the guards are live and not a silently-dropped typo'd variant — the one real failure mode for a class-only change; a full browser drive was judged low-value since the change is purely additive + reduced-motion-only (it cannot regress the default render) and the `transition-none` mechanism is already browser-verified from P5-8. **Deliberately deferred (the D89 resume point):** the ROOT CAUSE — the shared `glass.ts` button constants (`GLASS_GHOST_BUTTON`, `GLASS_ACCENT_BUTTON`, `GLASS_HUD_BUTTON`, `GLASS_NEUTRAL_BUTTON`, `GLASS_DIALOG_GHOST_BUTTON`, `GLASS_FILTER_TOGGLE`, `GLASS_INPUT`) all carry `transition-*` + `active:scale-95` with no reduced-motion guard and feed EVERY glass button app-wide, so the same defect still lives outside the P5 surfaces; adding `motion-reduce:transition-none` INTO those constants would fix the whole app in one additive edit, but it reverses this decision's call-site placement and reaches well beyond the P5 scope, so it's a deliberate app-wide pass worth the user's nod. *Why: the resume point scoped this to the three P5 surfaces and D88 set the call-site precedent; honouring that keeps the slice small, low-risk and non-reversing, while the root-cause `glass.ts` fix is flagged loudly as the natural, bigger follow-up rather than silently smuggled into a "P5 surfaces" slice.* **REVERSED by D90 (P5-10) — the constant-level guard was done and the call-site placement is no longer the precedent for these constants.** (2026-07-27) |
| D90 | Guard `prefers-reduced-motion` at the SOURCE — put `motion-reduce:transition-none` INTO the shared `glass.ts` constants, reversing D88/D89's call-site placement (P5 polish, increment P5-10) | The root cause D89 flagged and wrote up as its resume point, now fixed. The seven `glass.ts` constants that carry a transition — `GLASS_HUD_BUTTON`, `GLASS_GHOST_BUTTON`, `GLASS_DIALOG_GHOST_BUTTON`, `GLASS_ACCENT_BUTTON`, `GLASS_NEUTRAL_BUTTON`, `GLASS_FILTER_TOGGLE` (all `transition-all` + `active:scale-95`) and `GLASS_INPUT` (`transition-colors`) — each got `motion-reduce:transition-none` appended, so EVERY glass control app-wide (auth, lobby HUD, filters, decks, dialogs, corner controls) respects reduced motion from the constant rather than each call site; one additive edit covers the whole app. Under reduced motion the fade is off and the `active:scale-95` SNAPS rather than animating — the same behaviour `CoverDialog`'s `TILE_BASE` was browser-verified with in P5-8, so this is not a new interaction, only a wider one. **This REVERSES D88/D89's "patch at the call site" placement** for these constants; the reversal is deliberate and was named as the blessed next step in D89's own resume point, so it is a trailed reversal, not a silent one. A header comment in `glass.ts` now states the invariant ("every constant with a `transition-*` also carries `motion-reduce:transition-none`") so the next author keeps new transitional constants guarded. **Because the constant now supplies the guard, the four call-site guards that sat adjacent to a glass constant became redundant and were dropped:** `CardDetailDialog` Retry (`GLASS_GHOST_BUTTON`), `Settings` Back-to-home (`GLASS_GHOST_BUTTON`), `CoverDialog` Done (`GLASS_DIALOG_GHOST_BUTTON`), `ProfileSection` Save (`GLASS_ACCENT_BUTTON`). **Every call-site guard protecting an OWN non-constant transition was KEPT** — `Settings` font `<select>` + back-arrow icon slide, `CoverDialog` `TILE_BASE` + close button, `CardDetailDialog` close button, `CardGrid` info button, `ProfileSection` sign-in link, and the Save spinner's `motion-reduce:animate-none` (a `transition-none` cannot stop an `animate-spin`). Pure CSS-class slice — no logic/component/API/DB/schema touch; 1941 → 1941 tests (nothing new to unit-test: `motion-reduce:*` isn't observable in jsdom and className assertions are brittle). `bun run check` green (137 files / 1941 tests); engine rules unchanged (0.41.0). **Verified via the shipped stylesheet, not a browser drive:** a production `vite build` emits `.motion-reduce\:transition-none{transition-property:none}` (beside `.motion-reduce\:animate-none`) inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion:reduce)` in the main `index-*.css` bundle — the shared chunk where the glass buttons live — proving the guard is live, not a silently-dropped typo'd variant. A browser drive was judged low-value: the change is purely additive + reduced-motion-only (cannot regress the default render), the mechanism is browser-verified from P5-8, and the constant-vs-call-site placement is invisible in the compiled CSS (cascade is by stylesheet order, not class-attribute order, so moving the class from the call site into the constant string cannot change the result). *Why: D89 deliberately chose the small call-site slice and flagged the root-cause constant fix as the natural follow-up "worth the user's nod (or a considered autonomous slice)"; the autoloop resume point picked it up as that considered slice. Fixing the source and dropping the now-redundant per-call-site guards leaves ONE place the reduced-motion guard lives for glass controls, which is more maintainable than N call sites drifting out of sync — the exact reason these constants exist. With P5-10, P5's autonomous surface is exhausted: the only open P5 items (uploaded avatars, the remote P4 deploy) both need the user.* (2026-07-27) |

## Locked assumptions (override explicitly if they change)
- Bun-workspace monorepo; API + Lobby DO on Cloudflare **Workers** via `wrangler`.
- **Hono** + **Zod**; **Drizzle** over D1. Ingest uses **plain REST fetch +
  our Zod schemas** — the official `@tcgdex/sdk` turned out unnecessary since
  we validate every payload ourselves anyway (changed 2026-07-09, was: SDK).
- Server **sessions** (http-only cookie), not stateless JWT.
- Ingest filters to SV-era but writes the full-history schema.
- attacks/weaknesses/resistances stored as JSON columns for now (promote to
  child tables only if we need to query inside them).
- English (`en`) first; schema leaves room for i18n later.
- The **match engine (P3)** is the actual gameplay; approximate at first,
  improved iteratively.

## These are defaults, not law
Every decision and assumption here is a **default with a rationale**, chosen with
the context available at the time — revisit any of them when the code or new
context reveals a better path. The point of writing them down is to preserve the
*why*, so a later session can judge whether it still holds.

## Adding / changing a decision
Append a row (or a dated subsection for bigger ones) with the choice **and the
one-line why**. When you revise an existing decision, update its row and note
what changed and why. The one hard rule: **don't reverse a decision silently** —
leave a trail so the reasoning is never lost.

+| D91 | Defiance Band — a CONDITIONAL passive damage bonus, the D40 `BoardCondition` vocabulary's third consumer (P3-M5, engine 0.42.0) | The `conditionalDamageBonus` backlog row's first card, and the first PASSIVE reader of the D40 vocabulary — the conditional twin of Vitality Band ("If you have more Prize cards remaining than your opponent, the attacks of the Pokémon this card is attached to do 30 more damage to your opponent's Active Pokémon (before applying Weakness and Resistance)", sv01-169). **A card row + one new field, not a new primitive**, because it REUSES the existing `morePrizesThanOpponent` condition (added at D40 and already read by Fighting Au Lait's play gate + a branch op — this is the same predicate as a passive). `PassiveEffects` gains **`damageBonusBeforeWRIf: { amount, cond: BoardCondition }`**. **The load-bearing design call: WHERE the condition is evaluated.** continuous.ts's `passivesOf` is the single continuous-modifier aggregation point but is SEAT-FREE (it takes only `state` + the Pokémon), and a `BoardCondition` is seat-relative (whose Prizes?). a dedicated all-Basic deck is mulligan-free and seed-independent (cards pulled post-setup by id). **No web/API/DB/schema touch** — damage bonuses are engine-internal, surfaced only via the `DAMAGE_DEALT` log event (no projection field), confirmed by an Explore map. engineVersion 0.41.0 → **0.42.0**; 1941 → **1945** tests (registration + applies-when-behind + no-op-when-level + the (30+30)×2=120 before-W/R pin). `bun run check` green (137 files / 1945 tests). **Self-reviewed, no independent reviewer** (a cheap, contained slice; the mechanism mirrors Vitality Band, already reviewed). **Remaining on the row: Choice Belt** (sv02-176) — a TARGET-TYPE gate ("…Active Pokémon V"), a different shape (not a `BoardCondition`, so not this field), its own slice. *Why: the resume point named this "the last cheap D40 reader"; it is cheap precisely because the hard part (the condition vocabulary) already exists — the only new engineering is deciding where a seat-relative predicate gets evaluated within a seat-free aggregation pipeline, resolved by splitting aggregation (continuous.ts, unchanged responsibility) from evaluation (interpreter.ts, beside the one evaluator) rather than threading a seat through six call sites or duplicating `conditionHolds`.* (2026-07-27) |

## Session summary — P3-M5: Defiance Band (D91)

**Slice picked:** Defiance Band (`sv01-169`), the "last cheap D40 reader" the resume point named. I chose it over the first-named Chien-Pao ex because the resume point itself flagged Chien-Pao as "its own session" (a compound + pre-damage park), and this is autoloop iteration 4/5 — the smallest coherent green unit was the right call.

**What it is:** A Tool that adds +30 damage before Weakness/Resistance *while you have more Prize cards remaining than your opponent* — the conditional twin of Vitality Band, and the third consumer (first **passive** one) of the D40 `BoardCondition` vocabulary. Because it reuses the existing `morePrizesThanOpponent` condition, it was a card row + one new `PassiveEffects` field, not a new primitive.

**The one real design decision (D91):** `continuous.ts`'s `passivesOf` is the single continuous-modifier aggregation point but is seat-free, and a `BoardCondition` is seat-relative. Folding `conditionHolds` in there would have created a `continuous ↔ interpreter` module cycle. I split the responsibility: `passivesOf` stays pure and collects the gated bonuses raw; a new shared `interpreter.ts attackerPreWRBonus(state, pokemon, seat)` does the fold beside the sole `conditionHolds`, called from the only two pre-W/R read sites (`attack.ts` main hit + `snipeActive`). Kept out of the unconditional `damageBonusBeforeWR` so defender/HP reads can't be miscredited.

**One course-correction:** my first attempt added the card to the shared `STADIUM_TOOL_DECK` — but that's a fixed-60 deck (`setup.ts` enforces `DECK_SIZE`), so the reshuffle broke a fragile opening-hand test used by 5 suites. I reverted it entirely and gave the tests a dedicated, mulligan-free `DEFIANCE_DECK` fixture that perturbs nothing.

**Verification:** `bun run check` green — 137 files / **1945 tests** (was 1941; +4: registration, applies-when-behind, no-op-when-level, and the (30+30)×2=120 before-W/R pin). Engine 0.41.0 → **0.42.0**. No web/API/DB/schema touch (confirmed by an Explore map — damage bonuses are engine-internal). Self-reviewed, no independent reviewer (cheap, contained, mirrors the already-reviewed Vitality Band).

Other cheap candidates noted: Saguaro, the remaining rider shapes. Chien-Pao ex stays flagged for its own session; the P5 user-gated items (uploaded avatars, remote P4 deploy) still need the user.
